title: Americans voted blue. How the world is reassessing the US.
text:
Americans voted blue. How the world is reassessing the US.
A shift toward the Democrats in U.S. midterm elections has significant implications for global alliances, partnerships, war, and peace.
American voters this week sent a stern midterm message, and there was no mistaking the intended recipient: the U.S. president.
But the world was watching, too. Key allies in particular. Their immediate reaction was relief that the opinion polls weren’t wrong this time. President Donald Trump – whose dismissive, sometimes truculent approach has frayed ties with longtime partners – suffered as chastening an electoral rebuke as predicted.
Yet as the scale of Democratic Party gains sunk in, two other contradictory emotions have taken hold. First, hope. Hope that the voters’ pushback against administration policies that pushed up the price of gas, diesel, fertilizer, and other commodities will nudge Mr. Trump to rein in tariffs and wind down his war with Iran. Both of these are at the top of allies’ wish list as well.
Around the world, friends and foes of U.S. President Donald Trump are watching the results of midterm elections and asking what they mean for global alliances, partnerships, war, and peace.
But there’s also a deep concern that Mr. Trump could go in the opposite direction. Because foreign policy is an area in which he will have largely unaltered room to act even without congressional backing, international partners are worried he might double down on tariff pressures and make good on preelection threats to “finish the job” in Iran. Their priority is to do all they can to steer Mr. Trump toward conciliation.
The widespread relief with which they watched Tuesday’s election returns roll in was evident in public remarks by at least some allied politicians.
A British Cabinet minister called the result “an enormous night for American democracy, and for the Democrats,” while a vice president of the European Union’s Parliament said she felt “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf.” Norwegian Foreign Minister Jonas Gahr Støre welcomed the “powerful political signal” from U.S. voters, adding that Democrats’ foreign policy positions chimed better with Norway’s.
The response from two other leaders who have been on the receiving end of criticism and political pressure from Mr. Trump was more pointed. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the midterm vote as a sign that the tide of right-wing populism was ebbing. He added that it was a rebuke to U.S. administration policies of “hate” and “climate denial.” South African President Cyril Ramaphosa saw it as promising a “new era in world relations.”
Most allied leaders, however, sought to avoid the risk of angering the U.S. president by appearing publicly to applaud his setback at the polls. They’ve been focusing instead on the potential for a change in policy direction that might benefit both their own countries’ interests and Mr. Trump’s political standing.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the world “has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all ... the cost of living.” That was impossible, he said, “until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.”
America’s Gulf allies avoided public comment on the result, intent on maximizing the chances their diplomatic contacts with both sides, so far fruitless, might now move forward. Reuters, citing “two sources familiar with Gulf government thinking,” reported on the expectation that Mr. Trump would now have “more reason than ever to seek a peace deal.”
But that goal, and allies’ hope for a broader shift in Mr. Trump’s foreign policy priorities, might end up depending on another group of overseas politicians that was also monitoring the midterm vote: America’s rivals and foes.
The prospects for a negotiated end to the Iran war will hinge not only on Mr. Trump’s readiness to choose diplomacy over “finishing the job” militarily. Tehran also would need to be ready to make a deal.
Iran’s initial response to the elections suggests it saw American voters’ rebuke as having strengthened its hand – and weakened Mr. Trump’s – by highlighting opposition to the war. Russia, too, appears to have been emboldened by the result. Its deputy foreign minister dismissed the “short-term” significance of the gains by a Democratic Party he called “distinctly negative” toward Moscow.
Ahead of scheduled talks next week between Mr. Trump’s envoys and Russian and Ukrainian representatives, there was no sign the Kremlin was ready to alter its territorial demands for ending the conflict resulting from its 2022 full-scale invasion.
The broad outlines of possible deals for the wars in Ukraine and Iran have long been clear. On Ukraine, it would include at least de facto acceptance by Kyiv of Russia’s hold on the roughly one-fifth of the country it has taken by force, alongside credible American and European guarantees of Ukraine’s security against future Russian attacks.
On Iran, a deal would entail a firm, verifiable commitment by Tehran to halt its nuclear weapons program, as well as U.S. sanctions relief and economic support. But significant progress on either front, allies have long assumed, would require the assertive personal engagement of Mr. Trump.
And while the loss of the Republicans’ control of Congress need not constrain the president from acting on the international stage, another question raised by the election result might make that harder.
It’s whether the weakening of Mr. Trump’s political position at home will lessen the effectiveness of his trademark approach to foreign leaders: the swashbuckling self-confidence, the cajoling, the mix of carrot and stick.
And the degree to which these leaders feel the need to stay on his good side.
